questions.stem: How is the course made good found?
options: It is the direction of the current
It is the average of the compass courses steered
It is the true direction of the line from the departure fix to a later fix (or EP)
It is the course steered, converted to true
questions.explanation: The course made good is what the ship actually achieved over the ground, so it comes from two positions, not from the helm.

questions.stem: Two fixes are 15.0 nm apart and were taken 2 hours 30 minutes apart. What is the speed made good?
questions.explanation: Speed = distance / time = 15.0 / 2.5 = 6.0 knots. 2 hours 30 minutes is 2.5 hours, not 2.3.

questions.stem: Why can the course made good differ from the course steered, and speed made good from log speed?
options: Because of current, leeway and steering error
Because the chart scale changes with latitude
Because the course made good is measured in magnetic
Because the log always reads high
questions.explanation: Anything that moves the ship other than her own course and speed through the water shows up as a difference: current, leeway, steering error.

questions.stem: At 0915 a vessel has 24 nm to go. Her speed made good is 6 knots; the log reads 8 knots. What is the ETA, using the right speed?
questions.explanation: Time = 24 / 6 = 4 hours, so 0915 + 4 h = 1315. 1215 uses the log speed of 8 knots (3 hours), which ignores the current.

questions.stem: A destination is 27 nm away and you must arrive within 3 hours. What speed over the ground is needed?
questions.explanation: Speed needed = distance to go / time available = 27 / 3 = 9.0 knots. Compare it with what the vessel can actually do before accepting the plan.

questions.stem: Fuel consumption is 18 litres per hour. The passage will take 4 hours 20 minutes at that rate. How much fuel is burned, before any reserve?
questions.explanation: 4 h 20 min = 4.333 h; 18 x 4.333 = 78 L. 72 L uses 4 hours and ignores the 20 minutes; 86 L treats 4.20 as the number of hours.

questions.stem: A 20 nm passage burns 15 litres per hour. Planned speed made good is 8 knots, but a foul current cuts it to 5 knots. How much extra fuel does the foul current cost?
options: None, because the engine rpm is unchanged
questions.explanation: At 8 knots the time is 2.5 h and the fuel 37.5 L. At 5 knots the time is 4.0 h and the fuel 60 L. The difference is 22.5 L. Fuel depends on time, so a foul current costs fuel at the same rpm.

questions.stem: Which consumption figure should be used when planning the fuel for a passage?
options: The figure for full throttle, whatever speed you plan to run
The figure for the rpm and speed you will actually run, from the engine data or your own log
The lowest figure the engine maker quotes at any speed
questions.explanation: Consumption varies with rpm, load and sea state. Using a figure for a different speed gives a plan that is wrong in one direction or the other.

questions.stem: How big a fuel reserve must be carried according to the sources used for this course?
options: No reserve is needed on a coastal passage
Exactly 10 percent of the passage fuel
No fixed percentage is given; the skipper chooses a reserve, states it and records the reasons in the passage plan
Exactly one third of the tank
questions.explanation: The lesson sources give no required percentage for a small vessel. Some courses teach a rule of thirds, but what an examiner wants is a reserve that is stated and justified, covering weather, diversion and foul current.

questions.stem: A tank holds 500 L, of which 90 percent is usable. The engine burns 25 L/h and the speed made good is 8 knots. What is the range?
questions.explanation: Usable fuel = 450 L; endurance = 450 / 25 = 18 h; range = 18 x 8 = 144 nm. 160 nm uses the whole tank. 18 is the endurance in hours, not a range.

questions.stem: When should the ETA and the fuel remaining be recalculated?
options: Only if the engine alarm sounds
At each fix, using the new speed made good
questions.explanation: Current, wind and speed change as the passage goes on, so the ETA and the fuel check are updated each time a fix shows what the ship is really doing.
